ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

First-pass loss

A drug is well absorbed from the intestine but only a small fraction of an oral dose reaches systemic blood unchanged. The same amount given intravenously produces much higher exposure. Which process best explains this difference despite good intestinal uptake?

  1. Elimination before an IV dose enters systemic blood
  2. Presystemic metabolism in the gut wall and liver
  3. Complete failure to dissolve in the intestine
  4. Distribution into tissues only after intravenous dosing
  5. An obligatory lack of protein binding after oral dosing
Answer and explanation

Presystemic metabolism in the gut wall and liver

First-pass metabolism can remove absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.

Option explanations

Presystemic metabolism in the gut wall and liver: First-pass metabolism can remove absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.

Complete failure to dissolve in the intestine: The stem states that intestinal absorption is good.

Distribution into tissues only after intravenous dosing: Distribution occurs after either route and does not explain presystemic loss.

An obligatory lack of protein binding after oral dosing: Protein binding is not abolished by this route.

Elimination before an IV dose enters systemic blood: An IV dose enters systemic blood directly.
